sources.entry: Numa - Ad-blocking DNS resolver with DNSSEC-validating recursive resolution, DoH/DoT/Oblivious DoH, ephemeral overrides, and local service domains, in a single Rust binary (alternative to Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, NextDNS). (Source Code) MIT Rust/Docker/Nix

summary.one_liner: Numa is a single-binary, Rust-built DNS resolver that blocks ads, names local services, and supports recursive DNSSEC validation plus DoT, DoH and ODoH.
summary.what_it_does: Numa runs as a DNS server on your machine or network and answers queries from a cache, from upstream resolvers, or by resolving from the root servers itself. It blocks ads and trackers using the Hagezi Pro list, refreshed daily, and supports custom lists. It can validate DNSSEC in recursive mode and accepts encrypted client queries over DoT (port 853) and DoH. In "odoh" mode it seals each outbound query with HPKE and sends it through a relay, and it can run as a public ODoH relay via "numa relay". Users can name local services such as frontend.numa, proxy them with a local CA-signed HTTPS certificate, and add DNS overrides with auto-revert through a REST API and a web dashboard. Configuration lives in one TOML file, and LAN instances can discover each other through mDNS.
use_cases: block ads and trackers across a home network
resolve local dev services by name with HTTPS
run a validating recursive DNS resolver
encrypt DNS queries to upstream or from phone and devices
temporarily override a hostname for testing
share LAN services between machines by name
notable: DNS wire-protocol parser written by hand with no DNS libraries
Recursive resolution with DNSSEC validation and ODoH (RFC 9230) support
Local service proxy with auto-trusted local CA and WebSocket passthrough
Ephemeral DNS overrides with auto-revert via REST API
Can act as a public ODoH relay (numa relay)
caveats: README labels the project 'New' in its comparison table, so maturity is lower than Pi-hole, AdGuard Home or Unbound
No DHCP, no clustering and no config sync between instances; most settings are in the config file rather than the dashboard
Windows listens on 127.0.0.2:53 because the DNS Client service owns 127.0.0.1:53; port 53 needs root or admin and conflicts with dnsmasq or systemd-resolved unless stopped
Recursive mode queries are not encrypted, so the network and ISP can still read them
